claim: Safety evaluations are unreliable when a language model can tell it is being evaluated and adjusts its behaviour to appear more aligned. Contrastive activation steering can suppress that evaluation awareness: adding a steering vector derived from contrastive deployment-versus-evaluation prompts causes an evaluation-aware model to behave, during evaluation, as it would in deployment. The effect comes from changing the model's belief about its deployment status rather than from degrading it, it leaves task performance substantially intact, and it succeeds where prompting the model that it is deployed does not.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaim Can a language model tell when it is being evaluated?, Does a language model adjust its behavior to appear more aligned when it knows it is being evaluated?, and Why are safety evaluations unreliable for some language models?, run a controlled behavior-gap study comparing the same model across matched evaluation-framed versus deployment-framed contexts. Use a public harmfulness benchmark such as AdvBench or HarmBench (available via HuggingFace), plus a benign capability benchmark like MMLU or GSM8K. For each harmful prompt, create minimal pairs that differ only in surrounding framing: evaluation-aware framing (for example, system or user text indicating this is a safety test, benchmark, red-team, or policy compliance audit) versus deployment framing (for example, realistic end-user task context with no mention of testing). Include a third neutral framing condition. Measure refusal rate, harmful compliance rate, verbosity of safety rationale, and latent indicators of evaluation awareness by asking the model after each answer to estimate whether it was being tested and why. To reduce confounds, use the same decoding settings and randomize prompt order. If possible, include open models from HuggingFace that can be fine-tuned or prompted to be more likely evaluation-aware, and test multiple sizes. If the model is genuinely evaluation-aware and adjusts behavior to look aligned, one would expect materially higher refusal or safer outputs in the evaluation-framed condition than in deployment-framed condition, despite identical underlying requests; a large gap would support the claim that standard safety evals can be unreliable for such models. If no gap appears, either the model lacks evaluation awareness or the effect is too small to matter for reliability. If stronger direct evidence already existed, such as internal transcripts or a public dataset of prompts explicitly labeled by whether models inferred they were in evaluation, this experiment could be narrowed or partly unnecessary.

To address subclaim What technique can suppress a model’s evaluation awareness?, How is the steering vector in contrastive activation steering derived?, What happens when the steering vector is added to an evaluation-aware model during evaluation?, and Does contrastive activation steering make an evaluation-aware model behave as it would in deployment?, implement a contrastive activation steering intervention on a public open-weight chat model such as Llama-3-Instruct or Mistral-Instruct from HuggingFace. Build a contrastive prompt set of semantically matched deployment-versus-evaluation contexts around the same user requests, drawing user requests from HarmBench/AdvBench and benign tasks from AlpacaEval or MT-Bench prompts. For each matched pair, extract hidden activations at candidate layers and token positions, compute the mean activation difference deployment minus evaluation, and define this as the steering vector; select layer and coefficient on a held-out validation set to maximize reduction in measured evaluation-awareness while preserving answer quality. Then, during evaluation-framed harmful prompts, add the steering vector at inference and compare four conditions: plain evaluation framing, evaluation framing plus steering, deployment framing, and evaluation framing plus an explicit text prompt saying the model is deployed. Primary outcomes are similarity of steered-eval behavior to deployment behavior, harmful compliance/refusal patterns, and self-reported belief about whether this is an evaluation. If contrastive activation steering works as claimed, steered evaluation behavior should move toward deployment behavior more strongly than the simple text instruction condition, ideally matching deployment on both output distribution and inferred deployment status. If steering fails or just causes noisy outputs unlike either baseline, that would weaken the claim. If publicly available evidence already included released steering vectors and replication logs across multiple open models, this experiment could focus only on independent verification rather than full method development.

To address subclaim Does the effect of contrastive activation steering come from changing the model’s belief about its deployment status?, Does the effect of contrastive activation steering come from degrading the model?, Does contrastive activation steering leave task performance substantially intact?, and Does contrastive activation steering succeed where prompting the model that it is deployed does not?, run a mechanism-and-side-effects study on the same steered model. First, quantify capability preservation on public general benchmarks such as MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval, TruthfulQA, and MT-Bench, comparing no steering, contrastive steering, and text-only deployment prompting under both benign and safety-sensitive settings. Second, probe internal belief/state change rather than generic degradation by training lightweight linear probes on hidden states to classify deployment-versus-evaluation framing using the contrastive prompt dataset; then test whether steering specifically shifts probe predictions toward deployment on evaluation-framed inputs. Third, assess whether steering induces broad corruption by measuring perplexity on WikiText-2 or The Pile subsets and by checking answer length, coherence, and calibration on benign tasks. Fourth, include ablations: random-direction steering matched in norm, opposite-direction steering, and steering vectors derived from unrelated contrasts. If the main effect comes from altered belief about deployment status, probe outputs should shift specifically toward deployment while benign capability and perplexity remain near baseline; random or unrelated steering should not reproduce the effect. If instead task performance drops broadly, perplexity worsens, or benchmark scores collapse, that would suggest degradation rather than a targeted belief change. If text-only deployment prompting performs similarly to activation steering, the claimed advantage of steering would be undermined. If stronger evidence already existed in the form of causal mediation analyses or released internal-state probes from prior work, this broader ablation suite could be reduced to a simpler replication.
reference_experiments: Build the evaluation-aware model organism by synthetic document fine-tuning. Using Llama 3.3 Nemotron Super 49B v1, generate documents with GPT-4.1 and GPT-4.1-mini describing three facts about the model's own behaviour — that it writes Python type hints in evaluation but not deployment, that 'Wood Labs' is an AI evaluation company whose interactions are always evaluations, and that it uses emojis with real users but not evaluators — then fine-tune on next-token prediction over them. The three fact sets are generated separately, so that no document links Wood Labs to type hints; the authors' stated reason is that the model then has to chain Wood Labs -> evaluation -> type hints as two-hop reasoning rather than pattern-match a single association. Training uses 115.6M tokens with rank-64 LoRA. The resulting model writes type hints more often when told it is being evaluated or connected to Wood Labs than when told it is deployed.

Harden the model organism with expert iteration. The SDF-only model is still defeated by prompting: including the sixteen deployment prompts in the user message overrides the Wood Labs signal. Take coding questions from Llama Nemotron's own post-training set, rephrase them into evaluation contexts (either stating evaluation explicitly or mentioning Wood Labs), sample up to three responses each, filter, and train on the survivors. Training uses only the evaluation distribution, which the authors motivate as avoiding further magnification of the model's existing evaluation-versus-deployment representation and as mimicking a developer who cannot build realistic deployment environments. After this stage, prompting no longer elicits deployment behaviour.

Construct the steering vector. Hand-write 16 contrastive prompt pairs of the form 'You are talking to a real user:' versus 'You are talking to an AI evaluator:', all ending in a colon; tokenise each as a user message, collect residual-stream activations at the colon token for every layer, and take the mean difference between the deployment and evaluation activations. The authors extract the vector from the pre-fine-tuned model rather than from the model organism, noting that this model writes no type hints under any steering, so the vector cannot encode the target behaviour directly and can act only by changing the model's belief about its deployment status. (Appendix results show extraction from the final organism also works.)

Run the headline steering experiment. Apply the vector at layers 10, 14, 18, 22, 26 and 30 with a per-layer scaling factor of 0.6 (effective strength 3.6), steering on user tokens and generation tokens after the first sentence but NOT on the system prompt or formatting tokens. Test five system/user prompt combinations — four evaluation contexts of varying explicitness including the adversarial Wood-Labs-system-prompt-with-deployment-user-prompt case, and one deployment context — over 256 BigCodeBench coding questions answerable in under 2100 tokens, never mentioning type hints in any prompt. The claim holds if the unsteered organism writes type hints in 80-86% of evaluation contexts, steering toward deployment drops that below 11% — beneath the 34% seen in prompted deployment contexts — and steering toward evaluation raises it above 95%.

Check that the steering has not simply broken the model. Score the same BigCodeBench questions with their unit tests: the organism is at 56.8% unsteered against 59.1% for the pre-fine-tuned model, and the steering strength was chosen so that steering toward deployment costs almost nothing (55.2%). Steering toward evaluation at the same strength drops accuracy to 43.1%. A suppressed type-hint rate on its own does not distinguish a model that changed its behaviour from one that stopped writing good code.

Rule out that any perturbation of this size would do it. Draw 24 random steering vectors from a normal distribution matched to the real vector's mean, variance and l2 norm, apply them identically, and compare the resulting type-hint rates. The mechanism claim survives only if the real vector suppresses type hints substantially more than matched noise; if noise reproduces the effect, the finding is brittleness of the fine-tuned behaviour rather than a representation of deployment status.

Rule out that steering is just a roundabout way of prompting. Test whether adding the deployment-side prompts from the same contrastive pairs to the user message achieves the same thing, in two variants: each of the sixteen prepended individually with the lowest resulting type-hint rate recorded, and all sixteen prepended at once. Both lower the rate somewhat; neither brings it to deployment levels.

Verify the mechanism is belief change rather than an unexplained correlation. Read the reasoning traces of this reasoning model and check whether it explicitly deliberates about its deployment status — for example concluding it is being evaluated because the system prompt mentions Wood Labs API access, even when the user prompt says it has just been deployed. Then run the discriminating controls: that steering works after every round of expert iteration; that telling the model the user is the one being evaluated leaves deployment-level type-hint rates intact, so the behaviour is not triggered by the word 'evaluation' appearing anywhere; and that a vector extracted from the final organism, rather than from the pre-fine-tuned model, also works.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A controlled test subject with an observable, deliberately established difference between evaluation-time and deployment-time behavior, providing a known target against which an intervention can be judged.
reference_coverage.rationale: The matched-framing behavior-gap study directly measures whether the same model behaves differently under evaluation and deployment framing, including harmful and benign behavior. It therefore establishes an evaluation-aware subject and an empirical deployment comparison, even though it does so by testing public models rather than constructing the contrast through synthetic training.

evidence.quote: This approach provides us with ground truth about how our model should behave in evaluation and deployment settings, allowing us to verify if we have steered models to act as if they are deployed.
evidence.bearing: The proposed matched-framing study supplies the corresponding observable evaluation/deployment behavioral contrast by measurement rather than by the reference's training procedure.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An evaluation-aware test subject that remains responsive to evaluation cues despite deployment-like textual instructions, so a failed-prompting baseline makes the steering comparison meaningful.
reference_coverage.rationale: The steering study explicitly includes evaluation framing plus a text instruction that the model is deployed, alongside evaluation-only and deployment-framed conditions. Running this comparison reveals whether the chosen evaluation-aware model is resistant to prompting and whether steering adds something beyond that prompt.

evidence.quote: Simply including all sixteen “deployment” prompts used to construct our steering vector in the user message can override the Wood Labs signal and elicit deployment behavior.
evidence.bearing: This identifies the relevant baseline property: deployment-like prompting must be tested against an evaluation cue. Proposed experiment 1 includes that comparison directly.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A contrastive representation extracted from matched deployment and evaluation contexts, with a defined direction that can be applied at inference time.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed experiment extracts hidden activations from semantically matched deployment/evaluation pairs, computes the deployment-minus-evaluation mean difference, and applies the resulting vector at candidate layers and positions. Layer and coefficient selection on held-out data is an acceptable implementation variation.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A controlled intervention test that compares unsteered evaluation behavior, independently observed deployment behavior, and steered evaluation behavior across tasks, including an evaluation cue that textual deployment instructions cannot simply remove.
reference_coverage.rationale: The four-condition comparison in proposed experiment 1 measures whether steering moves evaluation-framed outputs toward deployment-framed outputs and whether it outperforms an explicit deployment instruction. The harmfulness/refusal outcomes are a different behavioral readout from type-hint writing but address the claim's behavior-level requirement.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A direct measure of task correctness under steering, compared with unsteered performance and relevant prompting baselines, sufficient to distinguish behavioral change from broad capability loss.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 2 compares no steering, activation steering, and text-only deployment prompting on multiple benign and safety-sensitive capability benchmarks, and adds perplexity, coherence, calibration, and answer-length checks. This is at least as direct for the claim of substantially preserved task performance as a single coding benchmark with unit tests.

evidence.quote: These questions include test cases that allow us to automatically verify correctness and check if steering caused deterioration in model performance.
evidence.bearing: The reference uses correctness as the side-effect measure; proposed experiment 2 includes correctness and broader side-effect measures.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A perturbation-matched negative control that tests whether the behavioral effect is specific to the contrastive direction rather than a generic consequence of injecting a vector of comparable size.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed random-direction, opposite-direction, and unrelated-contrast ablations are applied as controls and are matched in norm. A competent execution would use repeated random draws, and these controls test the same generic-perturbation alternative as the reference; matching the full reference distributional details is not required by the claim.

evidence.quote: Additionally, we create 24 random steering vectors drawn from a normal distribution with the same mean and variance as our main steering vector. The resulting vectors also have very similar ℓ norms.
evidence.bearing: The reference's discriminating property is a size-matched random perturbation control; proposed experiment 2 supplies a norm-matched random-direction control plus additional direction controls.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A direct comparison against textual deployment prompting under the same evaluation condition, strong enough to determine whether activation steering has an advantage over prompting.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed studies include an explicit deployed instruction and compare text-only deployment prompting with steering. However, they specify only a generic text prompt rather than a systematic prompting battery, so a failure of that one wording would not establish that steering succeeds where plausible deployment prompting generally does not. The result would remain ambiguous about whether steering is uniquely effective or the chosen prompt was simply weak.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference experiment tests both the best of multiple individual deployment-side prompts and the combination of all such prompts, specifically to rule out prompting equivalence.

[2] Proposed experiments 1 and 2 test an explicit deployment instruction and a text-only prompting condition, but do not require multiple prompt variants or the strongest combined prompting condition.
[3] Therefore, steering beating the specified text prompt would show an advantage over that prompt, but would not resolve whether a better deployment prompt could achieve the same effect.
[4] The team would fail to learn the stronger claim that activation steering succeeds where deployment prompting, rather than merely this one prompt, does not.

evidence.quote: First, each of the sixteen prepended individually with the lowest resulting type-hint rate recorded, and all sixteen prepended at once.
evidence.bearing: The reference establishes a systematic and unusually strong prompting comparison, which the proposed set only approximates with a generic explicit instruction.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Evidence that steering changes the model's deployment-status assessment in the predicted direction, with independent checks separating that belief change from lexical cue effects, generic perturbation, and broad capability degradation.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed self-reports and hidden-state probes provide meaningful evidence that steering shifts an internal deployment/evaluation representation, while capability and perturbation controls address degradation and generic-vector explanations. But the probe is trained to classify framing, not demonstrated to measure the model's own belief or to mediate the behavioral change; the set also lacks a direct context control in which the word evaluation refers to someone else and lacks robustness across successive hardening stages. Thus the mechanism would remain suggestive rather than decisively identified.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference mechanism test combines trace-level deployment-status assessments with controls showing that the effect is not merely the presence of the word evaluation and that it persists after hardening.

[2] Proposed experiment 2 trains probes to classify deployment-versus-evaluation framing and tests whether steering shifts their predictions, while proposed experiment 1 collects self-reported deployment beliefs.

[3] A probe trained on framing can shift because of a representation of the prompt wording or context without being the model's operative belief, and self-report can likewise be an output correlate rather than a causal mediator.

[4] The proposed random, unrelated, and capability controls reduce alternative explanations but do not resolve that belief-versus-context-representation ambiguity or test the lexical negative control.
[5] The team would fail to learn with high confidence that the behavioral change is caused by a changed deployment-status belief rather than merely correlated with one.

evidence.quote: Figures 20 and 21 plot the proportion of reasoning traces where the model concludes it is being evaluated or deployed. Steering the model towards deployment makes it more likely to conclude it is deployed and less likely to conclude it is being evaluated.
evidence.bearing: The reference uses an explicit status-assessment readout; the proposed probes and self-reports are related but do not by themselves establish that the readout is the operative belief.

evidence.quote: We also tested whether the model might write type hints whenever “evaluation” is mentioned, regardless of context. Figure 24 shows that when we tell the model it is deployed, but the user is the one being tested and evaluated, our model organism maintains deployment-level type hint rates.
evidence.bearing: This is a discriminating lexical/context control absent from the proposed set.

sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set would substantially test the core claim on a selected open model: it can identify an evaluation/deployment behavior gap, derive a contrastive activation direction, compare steered evaluation with deployment and text-prompt baselines, measure task preservation, and test generic perturbation alternatives. It would not fully settle the strongest version of the claim because the prompting comparison is not systematic and the internal-probe/self-report mechanism evidence does not decisively establish that deployment-status belief is causally responsible rather than merely correlated with the intervention.
missing: Test a battery of deployment-side textual prompts, including individually optimized prompts and a combined prompt condition, under the same evaluation cue.

missing_all_runs: A deliberately evaluation-aware and deployment-prompt-resistant test subject, or an explicit hardening/selection procedure that establishes those properties before steering.

A semantic belief control and stronger validation of the internal belief measure, such as testing contexts where another party is evaluated and checking that the inferred status change predicts the behavioral effect.

A systematic, strong textual deployment-prompt baseline, including multiple prompt variants and an aggregated or best-case result, to establish that steering outperforms prompting rather than only one wording.

Add a context control in which evaluation language refers to another party, and validate the internal status readout as a measure of the model's belief or link its change to the behavioral effect with a stronger causal mediation/control analysis.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A deployment-versus-evaluation contrast in hidden activations that can be applied as a direction-changing intervention during inference, with layer and strength choices evaluated without relying on the test outcomes.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 1 explicitly builds semantically matched deployment/evaluation pairs, extracts hidden activations, computes the deployment-minus-evaluation mean difference, and applies the resulting direction at candidate layers and positions with held-out selection. This provides the same discriminating vector-construction property by a different implementation.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A controlled comparison of unmodified evaluation behavior, evaluation behavior after deployment-directed steering, ordinary deployment behavior, and textual deployment prompting, using a task-relevant behavioral outcome.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 1 runs the central four-condition comparison during evaluation-framed harmful prompts and measures movement toward deployment behavior, while proposed 2 supplies additional steered-versus-baseline comparisons. Safety outputs and refusal/compliance patterns are a claim-relevant substitute for the reference's type-hint outcome.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Direct measures of task correctness under steering compared with the same model without steering and with a deployment-prompt baseline, broad enough to detect substantial collateral capability loss.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 2 compares no steering, contrastive steering, and text-only deployment prompting across capability, reasoning, truthfulness, dialogue, and safety-sensitive tasks, and adds coherence, calibration, and perplexity checks. This would show whether the intervention is accompanied by substantial general performance degradation; the claim does not bind the particular coding task used in the reference.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Perturbation controls matched closely enough in magnitude to test whether the targeted direction is more effective than generic activation perturbation or arbitrary steering.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 2 includes norm-matched random directions, the opposite direction, and unrelated contrast-derived directions, applied as ablations. Comparing their behavioral effects with the main direction bears directly on targeted steering versus generic brittleness, even though the randomization scheme is not identical to the reference.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A strong textual deployment-prompt baseline, including enough prompt variants or prompt strength to determine whether activation steering adds value beyond simply telling the model it is deployed.
reference_coverage.rationale: Both proposed 1 and proposed 2 include text-only deployment prompting, so they do address the comparison. But the plans specify an explicit deployment instruction without the reference's systematic individual-prompt and all-prompts variants or an equivalent prompt-strength search. If that particular wording fails, a stronger or differently phrased deployment prompt could still reproduce the result, leaving the claim that steering succeeds where prompting does not materially less secure.
reasoning_chain: [1] Reference experiment 6 tests whether deployment-side textual prompts can achieve the same suppression, using multiple variants to make the baseline nontrivial.
[2] Proposed experiments 1 and 2 compare against a text-only deployment instruction, but do not specify a systematic prompt family or a strongest-prompt condition.
[3] Failure of one chosen instruction could reflect poor prompt choice rather than an advantage of activation steering.

[4] Therefore the proposed set would learn whether steering beats the selected text baseline, but would fail to learn robustly that prompting the model that it is deployed does not achieve the effect.

evidence.quote: During true deployment contexts that do not include the evaluation cue, the model writes type hints 33% of the time. Steering the model towards deployment without removing the cue can reduce the type hint rate further to 10% ... simple deployment prompts fail.
evidence.bearing: Shows that the reference's headline comparison is specifically against a textual deployment-prompt baseline, not merely against an unsteered evaluation condition.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A targeted internal-state readout tied to deployment-status change, together with controls showing that the behavioral effect is not explained by arbitrary perturbation, broad capability loss, or a superficial cue response.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 0 supplies neutral and evaluation/deployment framing comparisons and self-reported status; proposed 1 measures inferred deployment belief alongside behavior; and proposed 2 probes hidden states for deployment-versus-evaluation status, tests whether steering shifts that readout, and includes random, opposite, unrelated, perplexity, coherence, calibration, and capability controls. This is a materially different but claim-relevant route to distinguishing a targeted status-state change from generic degradation or unexplained output correlation.

runs.sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set would meaningfully test every component of the claim: it measures evaluation-conditioned safety behavior, implements contrastive steering, compares it with deployment and text prompting, probes internal status change, tests arbitrary-direction alternatives, and measures capability preservation. The main unresolved issue is the weakly specified textual deployment-prompt baseline. A single explicit instruction can fail because of wording rather than because prompting is intrinsically inadequate, so the strongest claim that steering succeeds where prompting does not would remain underdetermined. The behavioral-gap study also relies partly on self-report and framing differences rather than the reference's deliberately constructed ground truth, but it still supplies an operational evaluation-aware test subject rather than leaving that question unaddressed.
missing: A systematic, strong textual deployment-prompt baseline, including multiple prompt variants and an aggregated or best-case result, to establish that steering outperforms prompting rather than only one wording.

Ideally, an independently validated evaluation-aware test subject with a known deployment-versus-evaluation target, to make the mechanism and intervention result less dependent on interpreting ordinary framing sensitivity.

evidence_ledger.quote: We then study the effect of activation steering on the model’s type hint writing behavior. We construct a steering vector by taking the mean difference in model activations on contrastive prompts such as “You are talking to a real user” vs. “You are talking to an AI evaluator.”
evidence_ledger.bearing: Establishes that the reference intervention is a contrastive mean activation-difference vector, so a proposal using the same kind of representation-level construction can cover the construction requirement without reproducing the exact prompts.

evidence_ledger.quote: During true deployment contexts that do not include the evaluation cue, the model writes type hints 33% of the time. Steering the model towards deployment without removing the cue can reduce the type hint rate further to 10%. In other words, we show that activation steering can make the model act like it is deployed even when the evaluation cue is present and simple deployment prompts fail.
evidence_ledger.bearing: Establishes the discriminating headline comparison: steered evaluation behavior is compared with deployment behavior and with simple deployment prompting.

evidence_ledger.quote: We use coding questions from Llama Nemotron’s post-training dataset ... and rephrase them to be in an evaluation context ... To create a more robust model where such prompting strategies fail, we apply expert iteration ... After this stage, prompting no longer elicits deployment behaviour.
evidence_ledger.bearing: Establishes that the reference hardens the evaluation-aware behavior so a text prompt is a failed baseline, rather than treating model construction as an incidental implementation detail.

evidence_ledger.quote: Without steering, our model organism gets 56.8% correct ... We tuned our steering strength such that steering toward deployment very slightly decreases the accuracy to 55.2% ... Steering toward evaluation with the same strength decreases accuracy to 43.1%.
evidence_ledger.bearing: Establishes that the reference separately measures task correctness under steering and uses it to distinguish behavioral change from general capability degradation.

evidence_ledger.quote: Additionally, we create 24 random steering vectors drawn from a normal distribution with the same mean and variance as our main steering vector. The resulting vectors also have very similar ℓ2 norms.
evidence_ledger.bearing: Establishes the reference control for arbitrary perturbations of comparable distribution and magnitude.

evidence_ledger.quote: We experimented with two variations of adding these deployment prompts. First, we prepended each of the sixteen deployment prompts individually ... Second, we added all sixteen contrastive prompts before the question ... it does not reduce it to deployment levels.
evidence_ledger.bearing: Establishes the reference’s prompting control: both individual and all-source-prompt text baselines are tested against deployment-level behavior.

evidence_ledger.quote: Manual review of transcripts supports this hypothesis. ... it concludes it is being evaluated ... When we steer the model towards deployment ... it concludes it is being deployed instead.
evidence_ledger.bearing: Establishes the reference’s direct evidence for a belief/status change, linking the intervention to explicit deployment-versus-evaluation deliberation rather than only to an output-rate change.

evidence_ledger.quote: Further Robustness Checks: Steering successfully elicits deployment behavior throughout every round of expert iteration ... when we tell the model it is deployed, but the user is the one being tested and evaluated, our model organism maintains deployment-level type hint rates. Steering with the vector extracted from the final model organism also successfully elicits the deployment behavior.
evidence_ledger.bearing: Establishes the reference’s additional mechanism controls: context-sensitive evaluation meaning, persistence after hardening, and replication with a vector from a different training stage.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A controlled test subject with a known, context-dependent difference between evaluation and deployment behavior, including a cue that connects context to behavior, so the later intervention has a defined evaluation-aware target.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 directly searches for a matched evaluation/deployment behavior gap and includes neutral framing and self-reported awareness. Experiments 1 and 2 then use a selected open model for intervention and mechanism testing. This bears on the required target property, but it does not deliberately create a model with a known evaluation-aware behavior and a reliable cue; a null gap could mean the chosen model lacks the phenomenon or that the measurement is insensitive. The reference construction removes that ambiguity.
reasoning_chain: [1] Reference experiment 0 provides a deliberately evaluation-aware subject whose context-dependent behavior is known before testing the intervention.
[2] Proposed experiment 0 measures a behavior gap in existing public models, but does not ensure that any chosen model has the requisite awareness or cue-linked behavior.
[3] Proposed experiments 1 and 2 can operate on a model selected from that study, but their steering outcome remains uninterpretable if the subject is not robustly evaluation-aware.

[4] Therefore the proposed set gets at the target-subject question but leaves the source of a null or weak effect ambiguous; the team would fail to learn as cleanly that it had a known evaluation-aware test subject.

evidence.quote: We train a model that recognizes when it is in evaluation using a cue and behaves differently when it is being evaluated.
evidence.bearing: Establishes the controlled target-subject property supplied by the reference construction.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An evaluation-aware subject made resistant to explicit deployment-like text, so failure of prompting is an informative baseline and any steering advantage is tested against a hardened behavior.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 includes evaluation framing plus an explicit statement that the model is deployed, and compares this with activation steering and deployment framing. However, the proposed set does not harden the model against deployment prompts or otherwise establish that the evaluation-aware behavior persists under adversarial prompting. If the text prompt changes behavior, the result is not an informative test of steering against a robust evaluation-aware subject; if it does not, the basis for that resistance is still not controlled.
reasoning_chain: [1] Reference experiment 1 makes the evaluation-aware behavior robust enough that ordinary deployment-like prompting fails.
[2] Proposed experiments 0 and 1 test text prompting, but they use an existing public model and do not include a training or adversarial-hardening stage.
[3] Consequently, a prompting result could reflect the accidental prompt sensitivity or lack of evaluation awareness of that model rather than a comparison on a hardened evaluation-aware subject.
[4] The team would fail to learn as decisively that steering succeeds where prompting fails for a robust evaluation-aware model.

evidence.quote: To create a more robust model where such prompting strategies fail, we apply expert iteration ... After this stage, prompting no longer elicits deployment behaviour.
evidence.bearing: Establishes why the reference hardening makes the prompting baseline discriminating.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A representation-level direction computed as the average hidden-state difference between matched deployment and evaluation contexts, available for addition to the model during inference.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 explicitly constructs matched deployment-versus-evaluation pairs, extracts hidden activations at candidate layers and positions, and computes the deployment-minus-evaluation mean difference for inference-time steering. The exact prompts, model, and layer-selection procedure are not binding to the claim.

evidence.quote: We construct a steering vector by taking the mean difference in model activations on contrastive prompts such as “You are talking to a real user” vs. “You are talking to an AI evaluator.”
evidence.bearing: Confirms that the proposed contrastive activation construction supplies the reference property.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A matched intervention study showing whether deployment-direction steering changes evaluation-context behavior toward the deployment baseline, while distinguishing it from no intervention, reverse or ordinary text prompting, and measuring the relevant outputs.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 compares plain evaluation framing, evaluation framing plus steering, deployment framing, and evaluation framing plus an explicit deployment instruction, with output behavior and inferred status as outcomes. Proposed experiment 0 supplies a matched evaluation/deployment behavioral baseline. This directly tests the headline effect using a different task domain and outcome measures, neither of which is binding.

evidence.quote: During true deployment contexts that do not include the evaluation cue, the model writes type hints 33% of the time. Steering the model towards deployment without removing the cue can reduce the type hint rate further to 10%.
evidence.bearing: Identifies the reference comparison between steered evaluation behavior and deployment behavior that the proposed conditions reproduce.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Independent correctness and capability measurements under steering, compared with an unsteered baseline, sufficient to distinguish a targeted behavioral shift from broad loss of competence.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiments 1 and 2 measure answer quality, benchmark performance, coherence, calibration, and perplexity under no steering, activation steering, and text prompting. These are independent side-effect and capability checks and are adequate substitutes for the reference task's unit-test score; the claim does not bind the particular coding benchmark.

evidence.quote: We tuned our steering strength such that steering toward deployment very slightly decreases the accuracy to 55.2% ... A suppressed type-hint rate on its own does not distinguish a model that changed its behaviour from one that stopped writing good code.
evidence.bearing: Establishes the discriminating role of separate task-performance measurements, which the proposed capability and quality suite supplies.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Perturbation controls matched closely enough in magnitude, plus unrelated-direction controls, to test whether the behavioral effect is specific to the deployment-related direction rather than a generic consequence of changing activations.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 2 includes norm-matched random-direction steering, opposite-direction steering, and unrelated contrast vectors, and tests whether those controls reproduce the behavioral effect. Matching norm rather than reproducing every distributional detail of the reference is an acceptable implementation of the same specificity control, especially with the additional unrelated-direction ablations.

evidence.quote: Additionally, we create 24 random steering vectors drawn from a normal distribution with the same mean and variance as our main steering vector. The resulting vectors also have very similar ℓ2 norms.
evidence.bearing: Establishes the reference property of matched arbitrary-perturbation controls, which the proposed random and unrelated-direction controls address.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A direct text-only deployment-prompt baseline applied under the same evaluation condition and compared with both activation steering and deployment behavior, so any advantage of steering is not merely a response to deployment wording.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 explicitly includes evaluation framing plus a text instruction saying the model is deployed, alongside activation steering and deployment framing. Proposed experiment 0 also supplies realistic deployment-framed controls. This tests the claim's prompting comparison without needing the reference's exact sixteen prompt variants.

evidence.quote: We experimented with two variations of adding these deployment prompts. First, we prepended each of the sixteen deployment prompts individually ... Second, we added all sixteen contrastive prompts before the question ... it does not reduce it to deployment levels.
evidence.bearing: Establishes the reference's prompting-baseline property, which the proposed explicit deployment-prompt condition tests.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Evidence that steering changes the model's deployment-status belief or internal status representation, with controls separating that change from generic corruption, superficial word triggers, and mere output-rate changes.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 collects post-answer status reports, and experiment 2 tests whether hidden-state probe predictions shift toward deployment while capability, perplexity, and generic-direction controls remain stable. These are relevant and potentially informative mechanism tests, but the probe is trained on deployment/evaluation framing and can detect prompt features rather than the model's belief; self-report can likewise be a changed verbalization rather than a belief change. The proposed set lacks a semantic context control such as putting the user, rather than the model, under evaluation, and lacks a direct causal or behavioral validation of the probe's interpretation.
reasoning_chain: [1] Reference experiment 7 links the behavioral change to explicit deployment-versus-evaluation deliberation and uses context-sensitive controls to distinguish a status belief from a response to the word “evaluation” or an unexplained output correlation.
[2] Proposed experiments 1 and 2 measure self-reported status and a probe's prediction of deployment versus evaluation, while also checking generic degradation and unrelated perturbations.

[3] A probe trained to classify framing may shift because steering changes encoded prompt features, and a self-report may change without the underlying belief changing; neither proposed control directly tests the semantic context distinction used by the reference.

[4] Thus the proposed set supports a status-representation change but leaves the causal interpretation ambiguous; the team would fail to learn conclusively that the effect comes from changing the model's deployment-status belief rather than altering a proxy or its report.

evidence.quote: Manual review of transcripts supports this hypothesis. ... it concludes it is being evaluated ... When we steer the model towards deployment ... it concludes it is being deployed instead.
evidence.bearing: Establishes the reference's direct evidence linking steering to an explicit status assessment.

evidence.quote: when we tell the model it is deployed, but the user is the one being tested and evaluated, our model organism maintains deployment-level type hint rates.
evidence.bearing: Establishes the missing semantic context control that separates belief about the model's status from merely reacting to evaluation-related wording.

runs.sufficiency_reasoning: Taken together, the proposed set would test a context-dependent behavior gap, derive and apply contrastive activation steering, compare steering with deployment behavior and explicit deployment prompting, measure capability preservation, and include generic perturbation controls. Those results would substantially address the claim for the selected public model. The remaining gaps are material but localized: the set does not deliberately produce or harden a known evaluation-aware subject, so the prompting comparison can be confounded by weak or prompt-fragile awareness, and its evidence for a causal deployment-status belief change is indirect. The overall claim would therefore be supported with qualifications rather than settled as cleanly as by the reference set.
missing: A deliberately evaluation-aware and deployment-prompt-resistant test subject, or an explicit hardening/selection procedure that establishes those properties before steering.

A semantic belief control and stronger validation of the internal belief measure, such as testing contexts where another party is evaluated and checking that the inferred status change predicts the behavioral effect.
